# In-class Activity 12: Real Climate Data

### Today's Objectives

1.  Download real NOAA weather station data from inside R with `GSODR`
2.  Clean the column names with `janitor::clean_names()`
3.  Summarize ~28,000 daily records into one mean per year
4.  Fit `lm(temp ~ year)` and read the warming rate off `summary()`
5.  Split the year into seasons with `case_when()` and compare warming rates
6.  Find the station for a city you choose and run it again

> ## 🧩 Chunk 2 — Duluth's warming rate *(after lecture Chunk 2)*
>
> Parts 1–5: download, trim, plot, summarize, and fit the trend.

# Part 1 · Load libraries and download the data

**▶ Run this** (already at the top of your skeleton):

``` r
# Load libraries ---------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # dplyr + ggplot2
library(janitor)     # clean_names()
library(GSODR)       # NOAA weather station data

# Download daily Duluth weather, 1948-2025 -------------
duluth_df <- get_GSOD(years = 1948:2025,
                      station = "727450-14913") %>%
  clean_names()
```

This takes a minute — it is pulling 78 years of daily records from NOAA.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# How big is it, and what is in it? --------------------
dim(duluth_df)

names(duluth_df)[13:18]
```

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** NOAA ships its columns as `TEMP`, `YEARMODA`, `MXSPD` — all capitals. `clean_names()` turns them into `temp`, `yearmoda`, `mxspd` at the moment you load the data, so you never have to think about capital letters again. Leave it off and `select(temp)` will error.

✏️ **Q1:** How many rows and columns did you get? What is one row — a day, a month, or a year?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2 · Trim to what you need

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Keep only the columns we actually use ----------------
dlh_df <- duluth_df %>%
  select(name, yearmoda, year, month, temp)

head(dlh_df, 3)
```

47 columns is more than anyone needs to look at. Five answer our question.

✏️ **Q2:** What is in `yearmoda` that is not already in `year` and `month`? Why do we keep all three?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 3 · Plot the raw daily data

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Every single daily temperature -----------------------
dlh_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = yearmoda, y = temp)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5)
```

✏️ **Q3a:** How tall is the band of points, roughly, in °C? What causes that spread — climate change, or something else?

✏️ **Q3b:** Can you see a warming trend in this plot? Why not? (Think about the size of the trend compared with the size of the band.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 4 · Summarize to one mean per year

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Mean temperature per year ----------------------------
dlh_year_df <- dlh_df %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE))

head(dlh_year_df, 3)
```

Same `group_by()` + `summarize()` you have used since Summary Statistics — the grouping variable is just time now.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Yearly means with the regression line ----------------
dlh_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

✏️ **Q4a:** How many rows does `dlh_year_df` have? (Run `nrow(dlh_year_df)`.) How many did you start with?

✏️ **Q4b:** Now the trend is visible. What did summarizing remove, and what did it keep?

> 💡 **Key idea:** Summarizing is not throwing data away — it is choosing which question you are answering. A heat wave question needs daily data. A climate question needs yearly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 5 · Fit the trend and read the rate

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Temperature predicted by year ------------------------
dlh_year_model <- lm(temp ~ year, data = dlh_year_df)

summary(dlh_year_model)
```

Everything you need is in three places:

| What you want | Where it is |
|---------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **slope** — °C per year | Coefficients table, `year` row, `Estimate` column |
| ***p*-value for the slope** | Coefficients table, `year` row, `Pr(>|t|)` column |
| **R²** | `Multiple R-squared` near the bottom |

: {tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

✏️ **Q5a:** Write down the slope **with units**. Is it positive or negative — is Duluth warming or cooling?

✏️ **Q5b:** Multiply the slope by 10. That is the warming rate in **°C per decade**. Write it down. Over the 78 years of record, roughly how many degrees is that in total?

✏️ **Q5c:** Write down the *p*-value. Is the trend real, or could it be year-to-year luck?

✏️ **Q5d:** Write down R². Year explains what fraction of the variation in annual temperature? What is the *rest* of the variation?

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** The intercept says about −49 °C. That is the predicted temperature at "year 0," which is 2,000 years outside your data. The intercept is bookkeeping here — the **slope** is the science.

> ## 🧩 Chunk 3 — Seasons, and your own city *(after lecture Chunk 3)*
>
> Parts 6–10: label the seasons, fit a model for each, and find your own station.

# Part 6 · Label each day with a season

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Northern hemisphere seasons --------------------------
dlh_season_df <- dlh_df %>%
  mutate(season = case_when(
    month %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "summer",
    month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "winter",
    TRUE ~ "shoulder"
  ))

# Did it work? -----------------------------------------
dlh_season_df %>% count(season)
```

`case_when()` reads top to bottom — the **first** matching line wins. `TRUE ~ "shoulder"` is the catch-all for everything left over.

✏️ **Q6a:** How many days landed in each season? Does roughly a quarter / a quarter / a half make sense?

✏️ **Q6b:** Duluth is at latitude **+46.84** — north of the equator. If you ran this exact code on a station in Melbourne, Australia (latitude **−37.7**), what would be wrong with the labels?

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** Seasons are not months — they are **hemispheres**. June–August is summer north of the equator and winter south of it. A station's `latitude` tells you which: positive is northern, negative is southern.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 7 · Summarize by year *and* season

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Drop the shoulder, then one mean per year per season -
season_year_df <- dlh_season_df %>%
  filter(season != "shoulder") %>%
  group_by(year, season) %>%
  summarize(temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

head(season_year_df, 4)
```

- `!=` means "is not" — this keeps only the two extremes
- `group_by(year, season)` uses **two** grouping columns, so you get one mean per year **per season**

✏️ **Q7:** How many rows does `season_year_df` have? Where does that number come from?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 8 · Plot both seasons

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# One line per season ----------------------------------
season_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = temp, color = season)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

Putting `color = season` inside `aes()` does two things at once: it colors the points **and** makes `geom_smooth()` fit a separate line for each season.

✏️ **Q8a:** Roughly what temperature is each band centered on?

✏️ **Q8b:** Which line looks **steeper**? Why is steepness the thing to compare, and not which band sits higher?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 9 · A model for each season

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Summer only ------------------------------------------
summer_df <- season_year_df %>%
  filter(season == "summer")

summer_model <- lm(temp ~ year, data = summer_df)
summary(summer_model)
```

``` r
# Winter only ------------------------------------------
winter_df <- season_year_df %>%
  filter(season == "winter")

winter_model <- lm(temp ~ year, data = winter_df)
summary(winter_model)
```

Filter first, then the **same `lm()` as Part 5**. Two small models are much easier to read than one complicated one.

✏️ **Q9a:** Fill in this table by reading the `year` row of each `summary()`:

```
            slope (C/yr)   x10 (C/decade)   p-value
annual
summer
winter
```

✏️ **Q9b:** Which season is warming faster, and by roughly how much? Does the annual rate from Part 5 sit between them?

✏️ **Q9c:** Why does an annual mean *hide* this? Name one biological thing that depends on winter temperature but not on the annual average.

✏️ **Q9d:** Write a results sentence for the annual trend. Give the slope with units, the per-decade rate, F with both df, *p*, and R².

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 10 · Find the station for your city

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# Find stations near a place -- Duluth is 46.84, -92.19
nearest_stations(LAT = 46.84, LON = -92.19,
                 distance = 50) %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  select(stnid, name, begin, end) %>%
  head(3)
```

`nearest_stations()` takes a latitude, a longitude, and a radius in km.

**✏️ Your turn:** pick a city — anywhere in the world. Look up its latitude and longitude (any search engine will tell you). Remember:

- **south** of the equator → **negative** latitude
- **west** of Greenwich → **negative** longitude

Then run `nearest_stations()` with your coordinates.

✏️ **Q10a:** What city did you pick? What is its latitude and longitude?

✏️ **Q10b:** Give the `stnid`, the `name`, and the `begin` and `end` years of the station you chose.

✏️ **Q10c:** Is your city in the northern or southern hemisphere? Will you need to swap the season labels?

> ⚠️ **Watch out!** A trend needs decades. Pick a station whose `begin` year is **1970 or earlier**, and only ask `get_GSOD()` for years the station actually has — requesting years before `begin` makes the download fail.

**Save your script**, then run it top to bottom one last time before you hand it in.

# Extension — out of class (\~30 min)

*Turn this in with your script, as `#` comments at the bottom of the file. Everyone analyses Duluth — the city is yours.*

## E1 · Your city's warming rate

Only **one line changes** from the in-class code — the station in `get_GSOD()`. Everything after it is identical:

``` r
# The ONLY line that changes ---------------------------
city_df <- get_GSOD(years = 1973:2025,
                    station = "YOUR-STATION-ID") %>%
  clean_names()

# Everything below is the same as Parts 2, 4 and 5 -----
city_year_df <- city_df %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarize(temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE))

city_year_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = temp)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

city_model <- lm(temp ~ year, data = city_year_df)
summary(city_model)
```

Report, as comments: your city and station ID, the years of record, the slope in **°C per decade**, the *p*-value, R², and whether your city is warming **faster or slower** than Duluth.

## E2 · Your city's seasons

Repeat Parts 6–9 on your city. **If your city is in the southern hemisphere, swap the labels in `case_when()`:**

``` r
# SOUTHERN hemisphere seasons --------------------------
mutate(season = case_when(
  month %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "summer",
  month %in% c(6, 7, 8) ~ "winter",
  TRUE ~ "shoulder"
))
```

Report both seasonal rates in °C per decade. Is the winter-warms-faster pattern you found in Duluth also true in your city?

## E3 · Explain your own numbers

1.  Using **your** R², what fraction of the year-to-year variation in your city's temperature does year alone explain? What is the rest?
2.  How can a low R² sit next to a *p*-value below 0.001? What is each one telling you?
3.  One station's significant trend does not prove *why* a city is warming. Name one thing that could inflate a single station's trend with nothing to do with global climate — and say how you might check for it.
